Sibyl has no hosted service of its own. Here is where your data goes: Voice and text go from the browser to your gateway, which sends them to OpenRouter for the models you chose. OpenRouter routes them to the provider behind that model. Connected apps (Google, Microsoft, Slack, HubSpot, Salesforce, MCP servers) receive what an action sends them, and only after an approval where the action changes something. Their tokens are encrypted in your secrets vault. Agent computers browse the public web from a sandbox on your server; private and local addresses are blocked. This guide takes you from a fresh clone to a spoken conversation with Sibyl on your own machine.

Node.js 22.13 or newer. Check with node --version . pnpm , through corepack. Corepack ships with Node and installs the exact pnpm version the repository pins ( packageManager in package.json ). You do not need a global pnpm. An OpenRouter API key. Create one at https://openrouter.ai/keys and add a little credit. One key covers chat, transcription and speech. A browser with a microphone. Sibyl's live conversation is built from swappable OpenRouter models, not a single vendor's realtime API. This page explains how a spoken turn flows, how Sibyl decides when you have finished, and what the measured latency looks like.

By default the browser streams your voice to the gateway over its WebSocket, and Sibyl's voice comes back the same way. Nothing else is needed. When the gateway has LiveKit configured ( LIVEKIT_URL , LIVEKIT_API_KEY , LIVEKIT_API_SECRET ), hands-free voice runs over WebRTC instead: the microphone and Sibyl's voice travel through a LiveKit room, and the gateway's room agent detects your turns with the same speech detector. The brain, the turn rules, barge-in, hedging and budgets below are the same in both. Transcripts, replies, visuals and approvals stay on the WebSocket. If the room can't be joined, voice falls back to the WebSocket. LiveKit also brings calls with several people and agents,

Your audio goes straight to an audio-native model, so it reacts to how you said something, not only the words. While you speak, the browser shows an instant caption from its own speech recognition (where available). This is only a display hint: the voice brain hears the real audio. After the turn, a transcription model writes an accurate transcript in the background, and the gateway replaces the caption with it ( transcript.update ).

The browser's voice activity detector ends a turn after 0.4 seconds of silence ( NEXT_PUBLIC_VAD_HANGOVER_MS ). That is quick on purpose, because turn merging handles people who pause mid-thought. Other safeguards: a turn starts only after 160 ms of sound, and turns with less than 200 ms of voiced audio are discarded; 400 ms of audio from just before speech was detected is kept, so the first syllable isn't lost; the detector calibrates to the room for one second and follows slow changes in background noise; while Sibyl is speaking, the speech threshold is raised 2.5× and new speech is ignored for 300 ms after playback ends, to avoid reacting to its own voice. All of these are adjustable; see

If you start speaking again within 3 seconds and before Sibyl has started answering out loud, the earlier fragment and its pending reply are dropped, and your whole thought is answered once. The browser is told with turn.merged .

Talk over Sibyl and it stops: the browser stops playback at once, and the gateway cancels the reply and any speech still being generated. A deep-brain gist that hasn't been spoken yet is dropped once your new turn starts. Measured time from you starting to talk to silence is about half a second.

Latency on shared provider routes varies a lot; the same model has been measured at 1 second on one call and 14 on the next. With HEDGE_REQUESTS=true (the default): if the voice brain hasn't produced a word after 1.2 s ( HEDGE_VOICE_AFTER_MS ), the same turn also goes to the fastest voice brain from a different vendor; if a speech segment hasn't started after 1.5 s ( HEDGE_TTS_AFTER_MS ), a duplicate request goes out on the same voice. Whichever answers first wins and the other is cancelled. A request that fails before producing anything fails over the same way.

Learning from live turns. In auto mode the gateway tracks each voice brain's real time to first word and uses whichever of the scout's top three has been fastest recently. A model you choose yourself always wins. Warm connections. Each session sends a small warm-up request to the voice brain, and provider connections are kept open for up to a minute between turns instead of Node's default four seconds. Small first segments. The reply is split into speech segments starting from about 14 characters, so the first audio starts sooner. Segments are synthesized in parallel. Gapless playback. Some answers are easier to see than to hear. Alongside its spoken reply, Sibyl can put a visual on screen: a chart, a table, a step-by-step plan, option cards or a short form. Visuals are written by the model in OpenUI 's openui-lang and rendered in the browser with OpenUI's chat component library ( @openuidev/react-ui ).

Typed messages are answered by the deep brain directly: text plus, when it helps, one visual. In voice mode , visuals come from the deep brain too. The voice brain hands off a task with @brain , and the deep brain answers with a short spoken gist and the visual. In single-model mode (no voice brain), the chat model writes both the spoken part and the visual. Greetings, small talk and short factual answers stay spoken only. Visual answers are on by default. Turn them off for everyone with GENUI_ENABLED=false , or per browser with Visual answers in Settings → Voice ( /settings/voice ). Without visuals the deep brain is asked for plain spoken text.

Every reply has two parts, in this order: A spoken part — one to three short, plain sentences that make sense without looking at the screen. No markdown, lists, code or URLs. When there is a visual, the speech gives the key takeaway instead of reading values aloud. An optional visual — exactly one fenced block tagged openui-lang , containing one complete program: We found three good options; the train is cheapest and only an hour slower. ```openui-lang root = Card([...]) ... ``` The model is told to write nothing after the closing fence.

h: How the gateway splits the stream
x: The gateway separates speech from the visual as tokens arrive ( SpeechUiSplitter in packages/genui ): Text outside a fence is speech. It is streamed to the browser as text and to the speech model in segments. Text inside a fence is the visual. It is streamed as ui.delta events and rendered progressively. Fenced code is never sent to speech. If a model forgets the fence and starts a line with root = , the rest of the reply is treated as the visual. Anything written after the visual (self-corrections, stray notes) is dropped. A second fenced program replaces the first, so a corrected version wins. Markdown symbols are stripped from the spoken text before speech.

On top of OpenUI's component reference, the prompt includes design rules that take priority. In short: Fit one screen. At most 8 top-level children and about 60 statements. One primary structure per answer: comparisons → a table (up to 6 rows and 5 columns); numbers over time or by category → one chart, with at most 3 key figures; multi-part plans → tabs, one per day or phase, each with up to 4 steps; how-tos → up to 6 steps; a few recommendations → a short list or option cards; gathering preferences → a form with up to 4 fields, structured inputs and sensible defaults. Short content. A title of six words or fewer, short text blocks, concrete values over adjectives, no filler sections. Real

Buttons and forms that continue the conversation become a new user turn. It shows in the conversation as the button's label and is sent to the model as [UI action] <label> , followed by the form values when a form was submitted. Links open in a new tab, and only http and https URLs are allowed. If a visual can't be rendered, the browser shows "This visual could not be rendered." and the rest of the reply is unaffected. Each assistant reply also has buttons to copy the reply, show the visual's source and ask again. Saved conversations keep their visuals, so you can reopen them from the history.
Visuals use Sibyl's light and dark themes through OpenUI's theme provider, including pop-ups such as selects and date pickers. They follow the theme you choose in the rail.

The deep brain can call tools while it works on an answer: built-in tools for everyday lookups, and any tools your MCP servers provide. Tools that only read run on their own. Tools that change something wait for your approval in the chat.

You ask something that needs fresh information or an action, by typing or by voice (the voice brain hands it to the deep brain). The deep brain decides which tools to call. Each call shows as a step in the reply ("Searching the web", "Reading a webpage"), with a short result summary when it finishes. The deep brain can take up to six rounds of tool calls, then writes its answer, with a visual when it helps. Long tool results are cut to a manageable size before they go back to the model.

Every tool is marked as either read or write : built-in tools are all read; an MCP tool is read only if its server marks it read-only ( readOnlyHint ). Everything else is treated as write. A write call pauses the deep brain and shows an approval card in the chat: what will happen, in a sentence or two, and the key inputs (long values are shortened and anything that looks like a secret is masked). With MODEL_SELECTION=auto (the default with OpenRouter), the gateway chooses models from the live OpenRouter catalog instead of a hand-maintained list. It runs at startup when there is no fresh cache, and again every 24 hours.

The scout reads OpenRouter's model listing, including the speech and transcription models. Voice brain: text-output models that accept audio input, with at least 32k context. Deep brain: models with Design Arena scores in the UI categories ( uicomponent , dataviz , website ) and at least 64k context. When five or more are benchmarked, the bottom half by UI score is dropped, so a very cheap model with weak visuals can't win on price alone. Transcription: models from established speech vendors only (OpenAI, Deepgram, ElevenLabs, Mistral, AssemblyAI, Google, NVIDIA, Microsoft). Voice: speech models that publish a list of voices. It skips free models, batch and alias routes, models that expire w

Each candidate's cost comes from OpenRouter's published pricing and a typical turn: Role Typical usage per turn Voice brain ~1,800 prompt tokens, 160 audio tokens, 80 output tokens (plus reasoning tokens if the model can't turn reasoning off) Deep brain ~16,000 prompt tokens, 1,300 output tokens (plus some reasoning) Transcription priced per second of audio or per token, depending on the model Voice ~160 characters of speech, priced per character, second or token The deep brain's prompt is large because it includes the full OpenUI component library (about 13k tokens). Models with prompt caching are noticeably cheaper there.
Quality is the mean Design Arena Elo for the role's benchmark categories: UI categories for the deep brain, speech categories for voices. Models without a benchmark count as slightly below average.

With SCOUT_PROBE=true (the default), the most promising candidates get small, real requests: Voice brains hear a real four-second spoken question with the real voice prompt. Reasoning is requested off; models that reject that are tried with low, then default reasoning, and are charged for it in the cost estimate. The result is the mean of two runs. Deep brains get the real deep-brain prompt. Voices start speaking three times; the slowest of the three counts. At most five probes run at once, so they don't slow each other down.

Four strategies weight quality, cost and latency differently. Each also has latency budgets: a candidate over its budget keeps only a tenth of its score, whatever its price, because no saving makes a slow voice feel right. Unmeasured candidates keep half. Results are cached in SCOUT_CACHE_FILE (default .model-scout.json ) for 24 hours. With a fresh cache, the gateway applies it before accepting connections. A full run sends a few dozen small requests, each with a short prompt or a few seconds of audio, so the cost is small compared with normal use. Set SCOUT_PROBE=false to rank on price and benchmarks only, with no probes.

h: What Slack sends and how Sibyl checks it
x: Every request carries X-Slack-Signature and X-Slack-Request-Timestamp . Sibyl computes v0= + HMAC-SHA256(signing secret, v0:<timestamp>:<raw body> ) and compares in constant time, before reading the body. Requests older than five minutes are refused (no replays). Sibyl answers within milliseconds; the agent's work happens afterwards. Slack's retries of the same event are recognised and dropped. The app's own messages, edits, joins and direct messages are ignored.

Meetings are calls where people and agents meet together, like a video call. Sibyl keeps the transcript, writes the notes as you talk, and finds the action items. Afterwards, the meeting has its own page with the notes, the transcript, playback and comments. Meetings are part of the open-source edition. Audio recordings of a meeting are part of Agent Serve. The room needs the realtime layer (LiveKit): see Realtime calls (LiveKit) to turn it on. Without it you can still schedule meetings and read the notes of past ones.

Meet at the top of a chat starts a meeting from that chat. Replies, visuals and approvals from the meeting land in that chat. Choose how Sibyl joins: as a participant (she answers when someone says “Sibyl”) or as a silent note-taker . sign-ins (and failed sign-ins), sign-outs; member role changes and removals, invitations, workspaces created and deleted; custom roles, role assignments and connection access rules; integrations connected, changed and removed, and app setup; secrets saved, deleted and used — by name only, never the value ; approvals, second approvals and every write action a tool ran; blocked tools and refused models; downloads (decks, files) and audit log exports; licence and policy changes, retention runs. Each entry has the time, who did it, the workspace, what it was about and the outcome (succeeded, failed or denied).

The log is append-only: Sibyl has no way to change or delete entries. Every entry also carries a SHA-256 hash of its content and of the entry before it. Check integrity walks the whole chain and tells you the first entry that was changed, inserted or removed (for example by someone editing the database file).

Export CSV or Export JSONL downloads the entries that match the current filters (newest first, up to 100,000). CSV cells that start with = , + , - or @ are prefixed with ' so spreadsheets don't run them.

Enter an https URL. New entries are sent in order, in batches of up to 100, as POST with a JSON body { "entries": [...] } and these headers: Header Value x-sibyl-timestamp Unix time in milliseconds x-sibyl-signature sha256= + hex HMAC-SHA256 of <timestamp>.<body> with your signing secret The signing secret is shown once when you save the webhook (or choose New secret ). It is stored in the secrets vault, allowed only for the webhook's host. Sibyl remembers the last entry delivered; after a failure it retries with back-off (up to 15 minutes) and shows the error. People sign in through your identity provider (IdP) instead of a Sibyl password. Sibyl supports OpenID Connect (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google, Keycloak, Auth0 …) and SAML 2.0 . Licence feature: sso .

Open Admin → Single sign-on → Add provider . Choose OpenID Connect or SAML, give it the name people see on the sign-in button ("Continue with Okta"), and list the email domains it signs people in for. Fill in the provider's details: OpenID Connect: issuer URL, client ID and client secret. Sibyl reads <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration when you save, so a wrong issuer is caught right away. Register the redirect URI Sibyl shows at your IdP. SAML: the IdP's single sign-on URL, its signing certificate (PEM), and optionally its entity ID. Register the SP entity ID and ACS URL Sibyl shows (or give the IdP the metadata URL). Press Check to test the settings, then sign in once in a private wi

OpenID Connect: authorization code flow with PKCE, state and nonce . The ID token's signature is checked against the IdP's published keys, plus issuer, audience and expiry. SAML: the assertion itself must be signed with the configured certificate. Sibyl checks the audience (its SP entity ID), the recipient (its ACS URL), the time window (one minute of clock skew), that the response answers a sign-in Sibyl started in the last 10 minutes, and that the assertion hasn't been used before. Sign-in started at the IdP (IdP-initiated) is not accepted. The browser that finishes a sign-in must be the one that started it.

A provider signs in people whose email is in one of its domains (a domain belongs to one provider). Claiming a domain is the admin's statement — one Sibyl is one organization, so there is no DNS check. An account already linked to the person at this provider is used. Otherwise an account with the same email is linked (OpenID Connect: unless the IdP says the email is unverified). Otherwise, with "Create an account the first time someone signs in" on, a new account is created in the workspace and role you choose under New people and groups . With it off, only existing or provisioned people get in. Accounts created this way have no Sibyl password.

Under New people and groups , map a group to a workspace role (for example engineering → Engineering, Admin). Groups come from the OpenID Connect groups claim (default groups ), the SAML groups attribute, or SCIM. People get the highest role their groups give. Leaving a group takes the role back. A role an admin gave by hand is never lowered. Groups never make anyone an owner.

Require SSO refuses password sign-in for every email in your providers' domains. One break-glass owner keeps password sign-in (with two-step verification, if you require it) so you can get in when the IdP is down. Turning on the requirement makes you the break-glass owner unless you pick another owner. Removing the last provider turns the requirement off. The owner token ( SIBYL_OWNER_TOKEN ) is an API key and always works.

SCIM 2.0 lets your IdP create, update and remove people and groups in Sibyl. Licence feature: scim . Open Admin → Provisioning (SCIM) and create a token. Copy it: it is shown once, and Sibyl keeps only its hash. You can have several tokens and revoke them one by one. In your IdP, set the SCIM base URL Sibyl shows ( <gateway>/scim/v2 ) and the token as a Bearer token. What Sibyl supports: Users list, filter=userName eq "…" (also externalId , emails.value , id ), get, create, replace (PUT), update (PATCH), delete Groups list, filter=displayName eq "…" (also externalId , id ), get, create, replace, update members (add, remove, replace), delete Paging startIndex , count (up to 200) Not supported

Under Admin → Session policies (licence feature sso ): Sign out after (hours): a session ends this long after sign-in, used or not. Without it, a session lasts 30 days from its last use. Sign out when idle (minutes): a session ends after this long without a request or chat message. Open chats are closed too (checked every minute). Allowed networks: IP addresses or CIDR ranges (IPv4 and IPv6). Sign-in and every request must come from them. A request from elsewhere is refused, but the session isn't ended, so it works again back on an allowed network. You can't save a list that leaves out your own address. Behind a reverse proxy on the same machine or private network, Sibyl uses X-Forwarded-For

Anyone can turn on two-step verification for their own account in Settings → Sign-in security , in every edition: it protects an account, and that shouldn't need a licence. What Agent Serve adds is requiring it for everyone. Codes are standard TOTP (RFC 6238: 6 digits, 30 seconds, SHA-1), so any authenticator app works. A code works once. Ten one-time recovery codes are shown when you turn it on. Sibyl keeps only their hashes. The secret is encrypted with the secrets key ( SIBYL_SECRET_KEY or data/secret.key ). If that key changes, people with two-step verification must use a recovery code, then turn it off and on again. A sign-in code request expires after 5 minutes or 5 wrong codes.

Sibyl is an open-source, self-hosted voice and chat assistant that runs on a single OpenRouter key. Everything ships in this repository; nothing depends on a hosted vendor service. It runs as two processes: apps/web — the Next.js web app: microphone capture, voice activity detection, gapless playback, the conversation view, visuals and approval cards. apps/gateway — a Node HTTP/WebSocket server: sessions, turn-taking, model calls, tools, storage, metering and model selection. It holds every credential. They talk over one WebSocket; see WebSocket protocol .

Each capability exists exactly once. New features build on these rather than adding parallel versions. Capability Lives in Contract Shared types: tools, approvals, storage, usage packages/core ToolDefinition , ToolRegistry , Store , UsageMeter Browser ↔ gateway messages packages/protocol WS_EVENTS , parseClientMessage , parseServerMessage Model calls (LLM, STT, TTS) packages/adapters LLMProvider , STTProvider , TTSProvider Voice/visual split, prompts packages/genui SpeechUiSplitter , VoiceReplyParser , prompts Persistence packages/store (SQLite through Node's built-in node:sqlite ) implements Store Brain: voice turn, deep work, tool loop, approvals apps/gateway/src/gateway.ts and apps/gatewa

Tools are ToolDefinition s registered in the one ToolRegistry . Read tools run automatically. Anything with effect: "write" (send, create, delete, spend) pauses for an approval card in the chat. See Tools, MCP and approvals . Every model call is metered through the UsageMeter with the actual cost OpenRouter reports, and checked against budgets before it is made. Credentials stay on the server. The browser never sees API keys or per-model request parameters. Protocol changes go through packages/protocol , with validation for everything the browser sends. Checks before merging: npx vitest run corepack pnpm -r typecheck corepack pnpm --filter @open-gpt-live/gateway build cd apps/web && corepack
Voice — the live pipeline, turn-taking and latency. Generative UI — how visuals are written, split and rendered. Models and costs — the model scout, presets and budgets.

The web app and the gateway talk over one WebSocket using JSON messages. All types and runtime validators live in packages/protocol/src/index.ts : WS_EVENTS — every event name; parseClientMessage — validates everything the browser sends before the gateway acts on it; parseServerMessage — validates everything the gateway sends before it enters browser state. This page describes each event. When in doubt, the TypeScript types in packages/protocol are the source of truth.

The browser connects to NEXT_PUBLIC_GATEWAY_WS_URL (default ws://localhost:8787 ). If ALLOWED_ORIGINS is set, the gateway rejects browser connections from other origins with HTTP 403. If SIBYL_OWNER_TOKEN is set, the connection URL must carry it as ?token=<value> ; otherwise the upgrade is refused and the web app shows its sign-in screen. On connect, the gateway immediately sends session.start and session.config . If the connection drops, the browser reconnects with backoff (0.5 s, doubling up to 8 s) and re-sends the user's saved model choices with session.update . Every message is a JSON object with a type . Most request-scoped messages carry a requestId , generated by the browser for type
